name: SOUTH SUDAN

flag.title: South Sudan Flag
flag.note: 3 stripes, blue triangle with gold star

lead: South Sudan became the world's newest country on 9 July 2011, when nearly 99% of its people voted to break free from Sudan. The White Nile winds through vast papyrus swamps, cool highland forests rise in the south-east, and over 60 peoples speak their own languages. A remarkable nation still finding its feet.
geo: South Sudan sits on a vast flat basin drained by the White Nile. The Sudd — one of Earth's largest wetlands — swells bigger than Belgium in the wet season, becoming a maze of papyrus reeds, floating islands and pelican-filled lagoons.

In the south-east the land climbs to cool forested highlands where Mount Kinyeti reaches 3,187 m. Six countries share a border with South Sudan: Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda, DR Congo and Central African Republic.
animals: The Sudd shelters the shoebill — a prehistoric-looking bird with a clog-shaped beak big enough to gulp a whole lungfish. The swampy flats are also home to the Nile lechwe, a chocolate antelope that wades chest-deep in water and lives almost nowhere else on Earth.

Every year around a million white-eared kob thunder across the Boma-Badingilo plains in one of the planet's biggest mammal migrations. Elephants, giraffes, lions and 400-plus bird species share this extraordinary landscape.
culture: The Dinka — South Sudan's largest group — are devoted cattle-keepers. A family's herd is its bank account and wedding gift. Young men can name their favourite ox by its exact horn curve and coat pattern.

Music and wrestling fill celebrations. Women stack beaded necklaces from chin to chest; men mark their foreheads with V-shaped scars showing community ties. Sorghum porridge and fresh Nile fish are everyday staples.
history: South Sudan's people fought for independence for over 50 years. When Sudan became independent in 1956, southern leaders were sidelined. A civil war raged on and off for decades, costing over a million lives and uprooting four million people.

Peace came in 2005, and on 9 July 2011 South Sudan raised its new flag — black, red, green and blue with a golden star — becoming Africa's 54th nation. Building stability remains a challenge, but its people's resolve is extraordinary.
wows: South Sudan is the world's youngest country, born on 9 July 2011.
The Sudd swamp grows bigger than England during the rainy season.
About 75% of the old Sudan's oil reserves lie under South Sudan's plains.
The Boma kob migration may involve a million animals, rivalling the Serengeti.
Over 60 ethnic groups live here, speaking roughly 60 different languages.
Mount Kinyeti's forests feel like a different world from the hot Nile plains below.
The shoebill stands 1.5 m tall and belongs to a bird family entirely its own.

myths.myth: South Sudan is all desert like the north
myths.fact: Most of the country is tropical: lush savannas, dense highland forests, and one of Africa's largest swamps cover the land — very little desert exists at all.
Oil helped fund the movement, but decades of cultural, religious and political exclusion drove the push for freedom long before large-scale oil production began.
